rule: Keep only the ASCII characters [A-Za-z0-9_-], in order, then keep the first 48 of them. Nothing is trimmed, normalised or replaced; an id that keeps nothing yields the empty string.
implementations: server/comfy-node/basrelief_depth/contract.py (safe_tag) — the node that CREATES the filenames
android/core/src/main/java/com/amoshydra/basrelief/core/depth/ComfyWorkflow.java (streamTag) — the app that MUST derive the same names
why: Both sides derive basrelief_<tag>_depth.mp4, _normal.mp4, .progress.json, .splat and .splat.json from this one string, and the app has to address files it was never told about. A one-character disagreement asks for a file that does not exist.

Every kept character is ASCII, so 48 characters is 48 code points, 48 UTF-16 code units and 48 bytes AT THE SAME TIME. That is what removes the old ambiguity: Python truncated 48 code points while Java truncated 48 UTF-16 units, so an emoji before the boundary made the two copies truncate in different places.

The empty tag is not an error and not a fallback here: the app refuses to submit one (isStreamTagUsable) and the node substitutes its own timestamp name, which the app could never predict. The rule itself has no fallback.

cases.why: a production UUID survives unchanged — this is the case that runs every day
an empty id keeps nothing; the app must refuse it rather than fetch a name the node will not write
space and slash are dropped, not substituted
underscore and dash are kept; order is preserved
leading and trailing dashes are KEPT — the rule drops characters, it does not trim edges
punctuation only keeps nothing, so the tag is empty rather than a placeholder
a dot is dropped, so an id can never smuggle a second extension into the filename
48 kept characters is the boundary and is INCLUSIVE; the 49th is dropped
an ASCII id longer than 48 truncates to exactly 48
truncation is by kept characters, and a kept separator counts toward the 48
a non-ASCII letter is dropped: the rule is ASCII alnum, not Unicode alnum
Roman numeral EIGHT is Unicode category Nl. Python's str.isalnum() ACCEPTS it and Java's Character.isLetterOrDigit rejects it — this fixture pins the ASCII answer, which both now give
SUPERSCRIPT TWO is category No: accepted by Python's isalnum(), rejected by Java. The ASCII rule rejects it on both sides
a supplementary-plane LETTER (Deseret, category Lo): Python's isalnum() accepts it, while Java's char loop sees two lone surrogates and drops both. Neither survives the ASCII rule
a combining acute accent is category Mn, not a letter, so it is dropped and not composed

THE TRUNCATION DIVERGENCE, at the boundary: 47 ASCII, then a non-BMP character, then 10 ASCII. Python truncated at 48 code points (47 a + the emoji); Java counted the emoji as two UTF-16 units and could stop mid-surrogate, emitting a lone high surrogate. The ASCII rule drops the emoji and keeps filling, so both answer 47 a + 1 b
the same divergence without the boundary: Python kept 24 emoji + 24 c (48 code points); Java kept 24 emoji (48 UTF-16 units) and no c at all. The ASCII rule drops all 24 emoji on both sides
a non-BMP character under the limit is dropped and the id continues — it is never replaced with a placeholder, which would make the two sides agree on the wrong string

names.why: The point of the tag: both sides derive these names from the id without ever having seen a response. The app fetches by them; the node writes them.
